# Chapter 12: Network Performance Tuning in Practice

Theoretical knowledge of the Linux network stack must be translated into concrete, reproducible configuration settings for production hosts. Misconfigured network parameters can cap a 100Gbps network link to 1Gbps, exhaust ephemeral ports, trigger bufferbloat, or crash a server under connection spikes.

This chapter details practical network tuning recipes, formulas for socket buffer sizing, congestion control selection, hardware multiqueue configuration, and validation methodologies.

## Core TCP Parameters and Their Effects

The following kernel parameters control connection lifecycle, backlog queues, and memory consumption:

```bash
# Increase backlog queues for incoming SYN packets and established connections
sudo sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096            # Max socket listen backlog
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=8192  # Max half-open SYN connection queue

# Reuse sockets in TIME_WAIT state for new outgoing connections (safe for clients)
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1

# Reduce TIME_WAIT timeout from 60s to 30s to free socket structures faster
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout=30

# Expand ephemeral port range for high-concurrency client/proxy hosts
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="10240 65535"

# Disable TCP slow start after idle to prevent latency penalties on idle connections
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0
```

## Socket Buffer Sizing Strategy

To maximize single-stream TCP throughput over long distances, socket buffers must be sized to accommodate the **Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP)**:

$$\text{BDP} = \text{Bandwidth (bits/sec)} \times \text{Round-Trip Time (RTT in seconds)}$$

### Practical Sizing Calculation

Suppose a 10Gbps link connects two data centers with an RTT of 40ms ($0.040\text{ seconds}$):
$$\text{BDP} = 10 \times 10^9 \text{ bps} \times 0.040 \text{ s} = 400,000,000 \text{ bits} = 50,000,000 \text{ bytes} \approx 50 \text{ MB}$$

If the maximum receive buffer (`tcp_rmem` max) is left at the typical default of 6MB, the TCP window will cap out at 6MB, limiting the maximum achievable throughput to:
$$\text{Max Throughput} = \frac{6 \text{ MB}}{0.040 \text{ s}} = 150 \text{ MB/s} = 1.2 \text{ Gbps}$$

The remaining 8.8 Gbps of link capacity will sit completely unused!

```bash
# Production tuning for high-BDP 10G/40G links
sudo sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=67108864          # 64 MB
sudo sysctl -w net.core.wmem_max=67108864          # 64 MB
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem="4096 87380 67108864"
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_wmem="4096 65536 67108864"
```

> [!CAUTION]
> On reverse-proxy servers handling 500,000 concurrent client connections, setting `tcp_rmem` max to 64MB risks instant kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes if buffer usage expands. High-concurrency edge nodes require smaller conservative buffer limits (e.g., 2MB to 4MB max).

## Congestion Control Algorithm Selection

Modern Linux supports dynamically loading congestion control modules:

```bash
# Enable BBR congestion control
sudo modprobe tcp_bbr
echo "tcp_bbr" | sudo tee -a /etc/modules-load.d/bbr.conf
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr

# Verify active algorithm
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control
```

- **Use BBR**: For WAN services, internet-facing APIs, cross-region replication, and lossy networks. BBR prevents packet loss from throttling bandwidth and maintains minimal queueing delay.
- **Use CUBIC**: For ultra-low-latency intra-datacenter networks where packet loss is near zero and packet queueing in switch buffers is tightly bounded.

## Multiqueue Configuration and RSS Tuning

High-speed NICs require symmetric allocation of queues across physical CPU cores:

```bash
# Check maximum supported vs currently configured hardware queues
ethtool -l eth0

# Set hardware queues to match physical core count (e.g., 16 queues)
sudo ethtool -L eth0 combined 16

# Increase NIC ring buffer sizes to absorb traffic bursts without packet drops
ethtool -g eth0
sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096
```

### Pinning IRQs with `irqbalance` or Static Scripts

Ensure that network interrupts are pinned to the CPU cores belonging to the same NUMA node as the PCIe slot hosting the NIC:

```bash
# Verify NUMA node of network interface
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/device/numa_node

# View current IRQ affinities for NIC queues
grep eth0 /proc/interrupts
```

## Validating Network Performance Changes

Never assume a network tuning parameter succeeded without rigorous verification:

```bash
# Test raw bandwidth and throughput using iperf3
# Server:
iperf3 -s -p 5201

# Client (multiple parallel streams to saturate link):
iperf3 -c 10.0.0.1 -p 5201 -P 8 -t 30

# Inspect TCP retransmissions, drops, and buffer errors during the test
nstat -z | grep -E "TcpRetransSegs|TcpOutRsts|TcpInErrors"

# Check for NIC-level packet drops and buffer overflows
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E "drop|miss|error|fifo"
```

If `TcpRetransSegs` or `rx_dropped` increment during the benchmark, the system is suffering from buffer starvation, interrupt drops, or switch-level congestion.
